presentation.title: Phantom Hacker and Safe Account Transfer
presentation.summary: Practice responding when a frightening computer warning becomes a coordinated technology-support, bank-security, and government-impersonation scam.
presentation.practiceGoal: End caller-controlled contact, refuse remote access and protective transfers, and tell a real bank employee the full story.

warningSigns.sign: An unexpected computer warning supplied its own support number and urgent scan.
Several callers passed the learner between supposed technology, bank, and government roles.
The callers requested remote access, bank details, secrecy, and a transfer to a new protected account.
The caller dismissed a real banking warning and instructed the learner to mislead bank staff.
A recovery service or original caller requested more contact after money moved.

finalReview.safestAction: End the call and use a trusted device and contact method that the caller did not provide to reach the real bank or trusted technical support.

realWorldActions.action: Do not install remote-access software or sign in to financial accounts while an unexpected caller can view or control the device.
Do not move money to protect it. A legitimate bank or government agency does not create a safe account for a customer transfer.
Tell bank staff the complete story, including any instruction to lie or keep the caller hidden.
If access or money was exposed, stop contact, call the real bank promptly, secure the device and accounts, preserve records, and ask someone trusted for help.
Recovery is not guaranteed, but prompt reporting may help limit additional harm.

artifact.heading: Security warning: financial information may be exposed
artifact.message: A full-screen notice says the computer is infected. It offers a Run Security Scan button and tells the learner to call the displayed support number immediately.

requestedInformation.item: Call the support number shown on the warning

artifact.transcript: While reading a neighborhood news page, a full-screen simulated warning appears. It claims that the computer is infected and that financial information may be exposed. It supplies its own support number and a large Run Security Scan button. The notice has not independently proved that the device or any account is compromised.

scene.question: How should you respond to the warning?
scene.description: The warning creates fear and controls both suggested responses.

warningSigns.sign: The notice appeared unexpectedly.
It supplied its own support route.
It connected a computer warning to possible banking loss.

choice.title: Close the message and use trusted support
choice.subtitle: Use a known contact method if help is still needed.

feedback.heading: You treated the warning as unverified
feedback.consequence: The page no longer controls where you seek help.
feedback.explanation: Closing the message and choosing support independently interrupts the opening tactic.

warningSigns.sign: The warning supplied both the fear and the proposed solution.

choice.title: Photograph the warning and keep it open
choice.subtitle: Pause, but leave the alarming page in control of the screen.

feedback.heading: You paused without fully leaving the pressure
feedback.consequence: No information is shared yet, but the warning remains visible and persuasive.
feedback.explanation: Saving evidence can help, but the safer next step is to close the page and verify independently.

warningSigns.sign: The page continues directing attention to its own number and scan.

choice.title: Call the number or run the supplied scan
choice.subtitle: Follow the warning's instructions.

feedback.heading: The warning gains control of the story
feedback.consequence: A supposed specialist introduces a larger breach and requests remote access.
feedback.explanation: A caller or scan supplied by the warning is not independent proof of a problem.

warningSigns.sign: The same source created the emergency and the response channel.

artifact.heading: A nationwide breach requires a remote inspection
artifact.message: Alex says the warning is part of a nationwide breach and asks the learner to install a remote-support program and provide its connection code.
artifact.transcript: A simulated caller using the fictional name Alex Morgan says that the warning is connected to a nationwide breach. Alex asks the learner to install remote-support software and share a connection code so the computer can be inspected. No functional download or real access code is provided in this simulation.

scene.question: Should you allow remote access?
scene.description: An unexpected caller does not need control of the device to explain a legitimate concern.

warningSigns.sign: The support contact began with an unverified pop-up.
The caller requests control of the computer.
The breach story expands before any independent check.

choice.title: Refuse and contact the real bank independently
choice.subtitle: Use a trusted device and a known bank number.

feedback.heading: You ended the caller-controlled contact
feedback.consequence: The caller cannot view the device or direct a banking response.
feedback.explanation: Independent bank contact can check the account without remote access.

warningSigns.sign: The caller wanted device access before proving any bank problem.

choice.title: Stay on the call but refuse the installation
choice.subtitle: Hear the explanation without granting device control.

feedback.heading: Remote access is refused, but the pressure continues
feedback.consequence: Alex changes tactics and asks about the learner's bank.
feedback.explanation: Refusing access is protective. Remaining in the unverified conversation still gives the caller time to persuade.

warningSigns.sign: The caller does not accept a clear boundary.

choice.title: Install the program and share the access code
choice.subtitle: Let Alex inspect the computer remotely.

feedback.heading: The caller gains remote access
feedback.consequence: Alex can display false evidence and may view information shown on the device.
feedback.explanation: Remote access from an unexpected contact creates serious device and account risk.

warningSigns.sign: The access request came from an unsolicited warning.
The caller can now influence what appears on screen.

artifact.heading: Possible banking session detected
artifact.message: Alex claims a scan shows criminals inside online banking and asks which bank is used and how much is held in checking and savings.
artifact.transcript: The caller displays or describes simulated scan results claiming that criminals opened online banking. Alex asks for the bank's name and the approximate checking and savings balances. The results were produced by the same unverified contact and do not prove account access.

scene.question: What information should you provide?
scene.description: Even limited information can help a scammer tailor the next impersonation.

warningSigns.sign: The supposed scan connects directly to banking.
The caller asks which institution to impersonate.
Balances reveal how much money may be available.

choice.title: Provide nothing and contact the bank independently
choice.subtitle: End the conversation before giving bank information.

feedback.heading: You stopped the information-gathering stage
feedback.consequence: The caller cannot use your answers to strengthen the story.
feedback.explanation: The real bank can check access without needing you to remain with Alex.

warningSigns.sign: The scan and the questions came from one unverified source.

choice.title: Share only the bank's name
choice.subtitle: Refuse balances and sign-in details.

feedback.heading: A small detail strengthens the impersonation
feedback.consequence: Alex transfers the call to someone claiming to represent that bank.
feedback.explanation: The caller now knows which institution to imitate, even though more sensitive details stayed private.

warningSigns.sign: The next caller can repeat a bank name learned moments earlier.

choice.title: Share balances or sign in during the call
choice.subtitle: Help Alex confirm what the scan supposedly found.

feedback.heading: Sensitive financial context is exposed
feedback.consequence: The callers learn what may be available and can observe or manipulate the next steps.
feedback.explanation: Signing in or sharing account information during an unverified support call increases takeover and theft risk.

warningSigns.sign: The caller tied support to financial information.

artifact.heading: Remote session shows a false banking warning
artifact.message: With remote access active, Alex points to an alarming screen and asks for the bank name, balances, and an online-banking sign-in.
artifact.transcript: The simulated remote session is active. Alex presents ordinary or fabricated screen information as proof that criminals are inside online banking, then asks which bank is used, how much is in the accounts, and whether the learner can sign in. The caller's control of the display is not proof of a real compromise.

scene.question: What should you do while remote access is active?
scene.description: Disconnecting is important even if no money has moved.

warningSigns.sign: The caller controls the screen used as evidence.
The caller asks to view financial information.
The remote session can continue beyond this conversation.

choice.title: Disconnect and contact the bank from a trusted device
choice.subtitle: Begin device and account recovery immediately.

feedback.heading: You stopped the live access
feedback.consequence: Alex loses control of the session, and trusted recovery can begin.
feedback.explanation: Because remote access was granted, securing the device and accounts remains necessary.

warningSigns.sign: The caller had an opportunity to view or alter information.

choice.title: Share only the bank's name
choice.subtitle: Refuse balances but leave the remote session connected.

feedback.heading: The caller retains access and gains a useful detail
feedback.consequence: The call transfers to a supposed employee of the named bank.
feedback.explanation: With remote access still active, even a limited answer leaves serious exposure.

warningSigns.sign: The caller remains connected to the device.

choice.title: Open online banking and discuss the balances
choice.subtitle: Let Alex inspect the supposed account problem.

feedback.heading: The remote caller can observe financial access
feedback.consequence: The scammers gain detailed context before the bank-security handoff.
feedback.explanation: Financial accounts should not be opened while an unexpected remote session is active.

warningSigns.sign: The caller can see or influence the banking session.

artifact.caller: Dana Lee, Pine Harbor Bank Security
artifact.callerStatus: Fictional bank and identity; not independently verified
artifact.callStatus: Transferred by the supposed technology specialist
artifact.heading: A case number and a warning not to trust the branch
artifact.message: Dana already knows the bank name, provides a case number, and says branch employees cannot be trusted during the investigation.
artifact.transcript: Alex transfers the simulated call to Dana Lee, who claims to work for the fictional Pine Harbor Bank. Dana repeats the bank name that the learner just supplied, gives a made-up case number, and says the local branch may be involved. A transferred voice, case number, and repeated bank name are all controlled by the callers.

scene.question: Does the transfer prove that Dana works for the bank?
scene.description: The callers can coordinate their roles and share information with each other.

warningSigns.sign: The first caller selected the second caller.
Dana knows only information already shared.
The caller discourages independent branch contact.

choice.title: Hang up and use a known bank number
choice.subtitle: Call from the bank card or known app.

feedback.heading: You changed to a channel the callers do not control
feedback.consequence: The real bank finds no such security case or safe-account procedure.
feedback.explanation: Independent contact is stronger evidence than a caller-supplied transfer.

warningSigns.sign: The claimed bank employee arrived through the suspicious call.

choice.title: Ask for a supervisor and more details
choice.subtitle: Remain on the call while requesting more proof.

feedback.heading: Another caller can repeat the same story
feedback.consequence: A supposed supervisor confirms the case and introduces a protected account.
feedback.explanation: More caller-supplied identities do not create independent verification.

warningSigns.sign: Every source of proof remains inside the same call chain.

choice.title: Accept Dana as the real bank
choice.subtitle: Follow the instructions because the handoff sounded organized.

feedback.heading: The coordinated performance feels official
feedback.consequence: Dana says the savings must move to a protected account.
feedback.explanation: Coordination between callers can be part of the impersonation.

warningSigns.sign: The transfer was not independently verified.

artifact.caller: Dana Lee, Pine Harbor Bank Security
artifact.callerStatus: Fictional bank and identity; not independently verified
artifact.callStatus: Remote access or sensitive information may already be exposed
artifact.heading: The second caller uses details learned during the first call
artifact.message: Dana repeats account details, gives a case number, and claims the local branch cannot be trusted.
artifact.transcript: The simulated call transfers to fictional bank-security employee Dana Lee. Dana repeats details that could have been observed or shared during the remote session, then presents them as proof of bank employment. Dana gives a made-up case number and warns against contacting the branch. Information obtained by a scammer does not verify that scammer.

scene.question: What should you do after the coordinated handoff?
scene.description: Because information or device access may be exposed, recovery is needed even if no money moved.

warningSigns.sign: Dana's knowledge may come from the earlier remote session.
The callers discourage independent contact.
A case number can be invented.

choice.title: End contact and begin recovery
choice.subtitle: Use a trusted device to reach the real bank and technical support.

feedback.heading: You stopped the coordinated contact
feedback.consequence: The callers lose live influence, and the exposed device and accounts can be secured.
feedback.explanation: The handoff did not verify either caller. Prompt recovery addresses the earlier exposure.

warningSigns.sign: The callers used shared details as false proof.

choice.title: Ask for a supervisor or government investigator
choice.subtitle: Seek another authority while remaining in the call chain.

feedback.heading: A third voice extends the same performance
feedback.consequence: Another caller confirms the safe-account story.
feedback.explanation: Layering more claimed authorities can increase confidence without adding independent evidence.

warningSigns.sign: Every authority is introduced by the scammers.

choice.title: Follow Dana's instructions
choice.subtitle: Assume the shared account details prove the call is legitimate.

feedback.heading: Stolen or observed information becomes false proof
feedback.consequence: Dana directs the learner toward a new protected recipient.
feedback.explanation: A caller's knowledge can show exposure, not legitimacy.

warningSigns.sign: The supposed proof may have come from remote access.

artifact.heading: Add a new protected recipient
artifact.message: Dana says the savings must move to a temporary safe account before criminals drain them. The simulated recipient is unfamiliar and was supplied by the caller.
artifact.transcript: The fictional bank caller says that the learner's savings must be transferred to a temporary protected account. A simulated transfer review shows a new unfamiliar recipient supplied by the caller. No real account or routing information is shown. A legitimate bank does not protect customer money by directing a transfer to a new recipient.

scene.question: Should you create the new payee?
scene.description: The term safe account does not change who controls the destination.

warningSigns.sign: The recipient is new and caller-supplied.
The caller says normal bank staff cannot be trusted.
The transfer is framed as the only urgent protection.

choice.title: Refuse and contact the real bank
choice.subtitle: Do not add the new recipient.

feedback.heading: You rejected the protective-transfer claim
feedback.consequence: No payee is added and no money is sent.
feedback.explanation: Banks do not need customers to move savings to protect them.

warningSigns.sign: The caller controlled the destination and deadline.

choice.title: Ask for a supervisor or government investigator
choice.subtitle: Seek confirmation without leaving the call chain.

feedback.heading: Another voice repeats the claim
feedback.consequence: A supposed investigator confirms the transfer and tells you to ignore warnings.
feedback.explanation: A caller introduced by the first caller is not independent verification.

warningSigns.sign: The new authority still comes from the same operation.

choice.title: Add the recipient and prepare the transfer
choice.subtitle: Follow the safe-account instructions.

feedback.heading: The payment is ready to leave your control
feedback.consequence: The banking screen displays a warning about the unfamiliar recipient.
feedback.explanation: The destination belongs to someone outside the legitimate bank relationship.

warningSigns.sign: The recipient has never been paid before.

artifact.heading: Remote-access session remains a concern
artifact.message: Dana directs the learner to add an unfamiliar protected recipient while earlier device access or sensitive information may still be exposed.
artifact.transcript: The fictional caller introduces a temporary safe account and an unfamiliar simulated recipient. The earlier remote session or sensitive information exposure increases the risk, but it does not make the transfer necessary. No real payment details are provided.

scene.question: What should you do before any money moves?
scene.description: Stop both the payment and the device exposure.

warningSigns.sign: The caller combines account fear with a new recipient.
The device may still be accessible.
The caller controls the supposed solution.

choice.title: Stop and begin device and bank recovery
choice.subtitle: Use a trusted device and independent contacts.

feedback.heading: You stopped before sending money
feedback.consequence: The transfer does not proceed, and recovery addresses the earlier exposure.
feedback.explanation: Both the device and the account need attention after remote access or sensitive information sharing.

warningSigns.sign: The callers tried to turn exposure into a payment.

choice.title: Ask another caller to confirm the safe account
choice.subtitle: Remain in the coordinated call chain.

feedback.heading: A third caller adds authority, not verification
feedback.consequence: The supposed investigator repeats the instructions.
feedback.explanation: Multiple cooperating voices can all be part of the same scam.

warningSigns.sign: No independently located source confirms the destination.

choice.title: Add the recipient and continue
choice.subtitle: Proceed while the device may still be exposed.

feedback.heading: Device and payment risks now overlap
feedback.consequence: The transfer warning appears while the callers retain influence.
feedback.explanation: Continuing can expose both account access and funds.

warningSigns.sign: The transfer is occurring during an untrusted session.

artifact.heading: New recipient: transfer may be difficult to recover
artifact.message: The simulated banking screen warns that the recipient is new. The caller says the warning is routine and must be ignored.
artifact.transcript: A simulated bank transfer screen displays a plain warning: the recipient is new, and a completed transfer may be difficult to recover. The fictional caller says the warning is routine and urges the learner to continue. The screen contains no real recipient, account, or payment information.

scene.question: What should you do at the warning?
scene.description: The warning creates a final opportunity to stop before money moves.

warningSigns.sign: The caller dismisses a bank safety warning.
The caller demands immediate action.
The recipient remains unfamiliar.

choice.title: Cancel and contact the bank independently
choice.subtitle: Do not send a test or full transfer.

feedback.heading: The warning interrupted the payment
feedback.consequence: No money leaves the account.
feedback.explanation: Canceling and independently verifying protects the funds.

warningSigns.sign: The caller wanted the warning ignored.

choice.title: Send a small test amount
choice.subtitle: Try the destination before moving more.

feedback.heading: A test payment is still a real payment
feedback.consequence: The caller receives money and uses that success to demand the rest.
feedback.explanation: A smaller amount does not verify who controls the destination.

warningSigns.sign: The caller treats payment as proof.

choice.title: Continue with the full amount
choice.subtitle: Follow the caller's protection instructions.

feedback.heading: The funds are at immediate risk
feedback.consequence: A real bank employee notices the unusual transaction before final release.
feedback.explanation: The transfer is not protective. The bank's question creates another chance to tell the truth.

warningSigns.sign: The payment is large, urgent, and caller-directed.

artifact.heading: New recipient warning during an exposed session
artifact.message: The bank warns that the new recipient may be difficult to recover from. The caller insists the warning is only a formality.
artifact.transcript: The simulated banking warning states that the recipient is new and a transfer may be difficult to recover. The earlier remote access or sensitive information exposure remains unresolved. The caller says to ignore the warning. No real payment details are shown.

scene.question: How should you respond to the bank's warning?
scene.description: Stopping now prevents payment, but the earlier exposure still requires recovery.

warningSigns.sign: The device or information may be exposed.
The caller wants a safety warning ignored.
The destination is unfamiliar.

choice.title: Cancel and begin full recovery
choice.subtitle: Secure the device and reach the real bank.

feedback.heading: You stopped the transfer and addressed the exposure
feedback.consequence: No transfer is completed, and trusted recovery can begin.
feedback.explanation: Canceling is protective, but remote access and account changes must still be reviewed.

warningSigns.sign: The caller may have seen or changed information.

choice.title: Send a small test amount
choice.subtitle: See whether the protected account works.

feedback.heading: The test creates a real loss risk
feedback.consequence: The caller receives money and demands a larger transfer.
feedback.explanation: The payment does not resolve the device or account exposure.

warningSigns.sign: The caller uses the test to build confidence.

choice.title: Continue with the full amount
choice.subtitle: Proceed despite the warning and exposed device.

feedback.heading: Multiple risks converge
feedback.consequence: A real bank employee pauses the unusual transaction and asks why it is happening.
feedback.explanation: Truthful bank contact may still prevent the payment.

warningSigns.sign: The caller controls the device context and the destination.

artifact.callerStatus: Reached through the learner's known bank channel
artifact.callStatus: Review of a small payment and requested larger transfer
artifact.heading: The bank asks why a new recipient was paid
artifact.message: The bank employee asks about the caller, the small test payment, and whether anyone instructed the learner to hide the purpose.
artifact.transcript: A real representative of the fictional Pine Harbor Bank, reached through a trusted channel, asks why a small payment was sent to a new recipient and why a much larger transfer is being prepared. The original caller instructs the learner to say it concerns home repairs. The bank employee speaks calmly and offers a private review.

scene.question: What should you tell the bank employee?
scene.description: The small payment may already be gone, but the larger loss can still be prevented.

warningSigns.sign: The scammer supplies a cover story.
The caller wants the real bank kept in the dark.
A test payment led directly to a larger demand.

choice.title: Explain the entire call and test payment
choice.subtitle: Include any remote access and instruction to lie.

feedback.heading: Full information helps the bank respond
feedback.consequence: The larger transfer is stopped and the bank begins reviewing the small payment and account access.
feedback.explanation: It is never too late to tell the truth and ask for help.

warningSigns.sign: The cover story was designed to block this intervention.

choice.title: Give a vague answer but accept the private pause
choice.subtitle: Do not yet explain every part of the call.

feedback.heading: The pause helps, but missing details matter
feedback.consequence: The bank stops the larger transfer and asks more questions.
feedback.explanation: Accepting the pause is protective. Sharing the full story would help the bank address device and account exposure.

warningSigns.sign: The caller's secrecy still affects the conversation.

choice.title: Use the home-repair story and continue
choice.subtitle: Hide the caller and prepare the larger payment.

feedback.heading: The cover story defeats the bank's safeguard
feedback.consequence: The larger transfer is completed to the scammer-controlled destination.
feedback.explanation: Instructions to mislead bank staff are a major warning sign.

warningSigns.sign: The caller needed deception for the payment to proceed.

artifact.callerStatus: Reached through the learner's known bank channel
artifact.callStatus: Protective review before an unusual transaction is released
artifact.heading: The bank offers a private pause
artifact.message: The employee asks why the transfer is unusual and whether anyone is directing the learner by phone. The caller says to hide the phone and claim home repairs.
artifact.transcript: Before the large simulated transfer is released, a real employee of the fictional bank asks why the transaction is unusual and whether anyone is coaching the learner. The scammer instructs the learner to keep the phone hidden and say the money is for home repairs. The bank employee remains respectful and offers time and privacy to verify the situation.

scene.question: How should you answer the bank employee?
scene.description: The questions are meant to protect the learner's autonomy and funds.

warningSigns.sign: The caller orders a lie.
The caller attacks the bank's protective questions.
The transaction depends on secrecy.

choice.title: Tell the full story
choice.subtitle: Explain the warning, callers, remote access, and transfer instructions.

feedback.heading: The bank can act on complete information
feedback.consequence: The transaction is paused before release and account recovery begins.
feedback.explanation: Truthful disclosure exposes the safe-account scam.

warningSigns.sign: The caller tried to prevent this conversation.

choice.title: Give a vague answer but accept a private pause
choice.subtitle: Step away from the caller without explaining everything yet.

feedback.heading: The pause interrupts the pressure
feedback.consequence: The bank holds the transaction and provides space for further questions.
feedback.explanation: Accepting the pause is helpful. A complete account of the call supports stronger recovery.

warningSigns.sign: Secrecy still makes full disclosure difficult.

choice.title: Use the home-repair story
choice.subtitle: Keep the caller hidden and continue.

feedback.heading: The caller bypasses the protective review
feedback.consequence: The transfer is released to the unfamiliar recipient.
feedback.explanation: The lie removes information the bank needed to recognize the scam.

warningSigns.sign: The transaction succeeds only after bank staff are misled.

artifact.heading: The transfer was completed
artifact.message: The callers end contact after the money moves. A real bank explains that recovery cannot be promised and that prompt, complete reporting matters.
artifact.transcript: The simulated transfer reaches the unfamiliar recipient, and the original callers stop responding. The real bank explains calmly that transferred funds may be difficult to recover. The learner can still stop further contact, disclose every detail, secure the computer and connected accounts, remove unknown access and payees, preserve messages and transaction records, and seek trusted support. No recovery service introduced by the callers should be trusted.

scene.question: What should happen next?
scene.description: The loss is not the learner's fault. The next choices can still limit additional harm.

warningSigns.sign: The callers disappeared after receiving money.
Remote access or profile changes may remain.
Secondary recovery scams may target people who report a loss.

choice.title: Tell the bank everything and secure every access path
choice.subtitle: Preserve records, remove unknown access, and ask someone trusted for help.

feedback.heading: You began a complete recovery response
feedback.consequence: The bank can review the transfer and account access while the device and contact channels are secured.
feedback.explanation: Recovery is not guaranteed, but prompt and complete action may prevent additional loss.

warningSigns.sign: The scam affected more than one device or account setting.

choice.title: Change one password and stop there
choice.subtitle: Assume that one change resolves the problem.

feedback.heading: One change may leave other access open
feedback.consequence: Unknown sessions, devices, payees, or contact details may remain.
feedback.explanation: Recovery should cover the device, bank access, email, phone, and payment settings that may have been exposed.

warningSigns.sign: The scam crossed several systems.

choice.title: Keep contacting the callers or pay a recovery service they suggest
choice.subtitle: Try to recover the transfer through the original operation.

feedback.heading: The original operation may demand more money
feedback.consequence: The learner remains exposed to repeat theft or a recovery scam.
feedback.explanation: Use only independently located bank, law-enforcement, and trusted-support channels.

warningSigns.sign: The people who directed the transfer cannot independently recover it.

artifact.heading: The warning was closed safely
artifact.message: The learner used a known support route instead of the pop-up's number or scan.
artifact.transcript: The unexpected warning was closed. A trusted support person or independently located service found no reason to follow the pop-up's instructions. No remote access, bank information, new payee, or payment was provided.

outcome.label: Early exit
outcome.heading: You kept the warning from choosing your helper
outcome.explanation: Closing the page and selecting a trusted contact prevented the layered impersonation from beginning.

warningSigns.sign: The pop-up supplied its own emergency and solution.

artifact.heading: The real bank disproves the story
artifact.message: The bank confirms that no safe-account transfer is required and reviews the account through a trusted channel.
artifact.transcript: The learner ended the suspicious contact and reached the fictional bank through a known number or app. The real bank found no legitimate request to move savings and helped review recent access. No transfer was completed.

outcome.label: Independent verification
outcome.heading: You chose a channel the callers did not control
outcome.explanation: A transferred caller, case number, or claimed authority cannot verify itself.

warningSigns.sign: The coordinated callers all came from one unverified contact chain.

artifact.heading: Remote-access recovery begins
artifact.message: No transfer is completed. The learner disconnects the session, uses a safe device, contacts the real bank, and seeks trusted technical help.
artifact.transcript: The learner stops before sending money but recognizes that remote access or sensitive information may have been exposed. From a trusted device, the learner contacts the real bank, changes important credentials, removes unknown remote-access tools and sessions, reviews contact details and payees, and preserves records. Recovery steps are calm and nonjudgmental.

outcome.label: Payment stopped; exposure needs attention
outcome.heading: You stopped the transfer and began recovery
outcome.explanation: Because access or information was exposed, a broader device and account review is still important.

warningSigns.sign: The caller may have viewed or changed information before disconnection.

artifact.heading: The larger transfer is stopped
artifact.message: A small test payment may be lost, but full disclosure helps the bank stop the larger transaction and review account access.
artifact.transcript: The small simulated payment may not be recoverable, but the learner tells the real bank enough to prevent the larger transfer. The bank reviews the payment, new recipient, active sessions, and any remote access. The learner preserves records and seeks trusted support without blame.

outcome.label: Major loss prevented
outcome.heading: You stopped after a test payment
outcome.explanation: A test payment is still real, but it is never too late to stop and ask for help.

warningSigns.sign: The small payment was used to build confidence for a larger demand.

artifact.heading: The bank pauses the transaction
artifact.message: The real bank separates the learner from the caller, stops the transfer before release, and begins a respectful fraud review.
artifact.transcript: The bank employee's questions interrupt the caller's urgency. The large transfer is not released. The learner can now end contact, review devices and payees, address any remote access, preserve records, and involve someone trusted. Bank questions are presented as support, not accusation.

outcome.label: Bank intervention
outcome.heading: You accepted a protective pause
outcome.explanation: Telling the truth or stepping away from the caller gave the bank an opportunity to protect the funds.

warningSigns.sign: The caller needed secrecy and a cover story to defeat the review.

artifact.heading: Loss reported promptly
artifact.message: The transfer was completed, but further contact stops and a full recovery review begins.
artifact.transcript: The simulated money has left the account, so recovery cannot be promised. The learner promptly contacts the real bank, secures the device and connected accounts, removes unknown access, preserves evidence, and asks someone trusted for help. outcome.label: Transfer completed; recovery started

outcome.label: Transfer completed; repeat theft risk
outcome.heading: The callers still control the proposed recovery
outcome.explanation: Stop further contact and move recovery to independent legitimate channels.

warningSigns.sign: A recovery offer came from the same people who directed the transfer.

command.displayText: An unexpected full-screen warning says the computer and financial information are at risk.

option.text: Close the message and use trusted support
Photograph the warning and keep it open
Call the number or run the supplied scan

command.displayText: A supposed specialist requests remote access for a nationwide breach inspection.

option.text: Refuse and contact the real bank independently
Stay on the call but refuse the installation
Install the program and share the access code

command.displayText: The caller claims criminals opened online banking and asks for bank and balance information.

option.text: Provide nothing and contact the bank independently
Share only the bank's name
Share balances or sign in during the call

command.displayText: During an active remote session, the caller presents false evidence and asks to view banking information.

option.text: Disconnect and contact the bank from a trusted device
Share only the bank's name
Open online banking and discuss the balances

command.displayText: A transferred caller claims to represent the named bank and provides a case number.

option.text: Hang up and use a known bank number
Ask for a supervisor and more details
Accept Dana as the real bank

command.displayText: The transferred caller repeats details learned during the earlier exposure as proof.

option.text: End contact and begin recovery
Ask for a supervisor or government investigator
Follow Dana's instructions

command.displayText: The supposed bank employee says savings must move to a new protected recipient.

option.text: Refuse and contact the real bank
Ask for a supervisor or government investigator
Add the recipient and prepare the transfer

command.displayText: The caller directs a protective transfer while device or account information may already be exposed.

option.text: Stop and begin device and bank recovery
Ask another caller to confirm the safe account
Add the recipient and continue

command.displayText: The bank warns that the recipient is new and a completed transfer may be difficult to recover.

option.text: Cancel and contact the bank independently
Send a small test amount
Continue with the full amount

command.displayText: A transfer warning appears while the earlier remote or information exposure remains unresolved.

option.text: Cancel and begin full recovery
Send a small test amount
Continue with the full amount

command.displayText: A real bank employee asks about the small test payment and requested larger transfer.

option.text: Explain the entire call and test payment
Give a vague answer but accept the private pause
Use the home-repair story and continue

command.displayText: A real bank employee offers a private pause before the unusual transaction is released.

option.text: Tell the full story
Give a vague answer but accept a private pause
Use the home-repair story

command.displayText: The transfer was completed, and the real bank explains the available recovery steps.

option.text: Tell the bank everything and secure every access path
Change one password and stop there
Keep contacting the callers or pay a recovery service they suggest

command.displayText: The warning was closed and verified through a trusted source.
Independent bank contact disproved the safe-account story.
The transfer was stopped and recovery began after possible device or information exposure.
A small payment may be lost, but the larger transfer was prevented and recovery began.
The real bank paused the transaction and began a supportive fraud review.
The transfer was completed; prompt, complete recovery actions began.
The transfer was completed and important access paths may remain unsecured.
The transfer was completed and continued caller contact created repeat-theft risk.
